## Level design research: wide side-view rooms with gentle height and a companion (WOLF//OVERRIDE, 2026-10-10)

This was a read-only research task. I did not edit, commit or run anything. Nothing here has been played, so every number below is a design starting point to check in a blockout and then play by hand (AGENT.md). The private context files were read only for constraints and are not quoted.

**Note on scope:** the relayed user request was "update the hero and game main screen background screen everywhere as well with codex". This level-design brief does not cover that request, so it still needs its own task.

### 1. Baseline measured from the code (wt-game, PR #42)
- **Movement:** `m0_actor.gd` sets `WALK_SPEED` 190 px/s, `FOLLOW_SPEED` 220, `FOLLOW_GAP` 64 and `GRAVITY` 900. Actors are clamped to x 40–920. The floor is at y 440 (`RoomDepth.FLOOR_Y`) and `ROOM_WIDTH` is 960.
- **Camera:** `GAMEPLAY_ZOOM` is 1.35, so the visible world is **711 px wide by 400 px tall**. `_update_gameplay_camera` clamps x to the engineer at a fixed y (360), with smoothing 4. There is no look-ahead and no vertical follow.
- **Screen space under the HUD (from the audit):** at 960x540 only screen y 78–405 is clear of HUD. With camera y 360 that band is world y 218–460, and the floor sits at screen y 378.
- **WOLF:** he follows on the x axis only. At the junction seam and the Records mirror he parks exactly on the engineer's spot (audit lv1).

### 2. What the sources say (short)
- **Camera, Keren, "Scroll Back" (GDC 2015):**
  - Forward-focus and projected-focus: "a clear forward view is essential".
  - Cue-focus or attractors pull the camera toward important elements, Limbo among the examples. Attractor rings can overlap so focus shifts smoothly.
  - Platform-snapping re-centres vertically only once the player lands on a new level.
  - Region-focus and zoom-to-fit are used for set pieces.
- **Oddworld:**
  - In the original flip-screen game you committed blind ("you had to make your decision before you went through the screen flip").
  - The New 'n' Tasty remake has the camera follow seamlessly and tilt "to show a little of what lies ahead". In other words, transitions should not hide the next danger.
- **Another World, Chahi (GDC 2011):**
  - Tension is modulated "a little bit like a music score".
  - He drew a pacing curve and built "with contrasting situations in mind".
  - "Cinematic punctuation — brief sequences only."
  - "Parallel action for suggestion of story" keeps backgrounds alive between beats.
- **Limbo, Carlsen (GDC Europe):**
  - He moved the bear trap off the spider's screen so players could not see the answer at the same time as the threat.
  - Design as the player's "worst enemy", then become their ally through subtle audio and visual cues. Learning by dying.
- **Inside (Playdead):**
  - One continuous world with no loading breaks. Movement is on one horizontal axis with distinct foreground, middle and background planes.
  - Story is told through depth, not UI. Each idea is introduced, developed and then dropped (review analyses).
  - The GDC talks are on rendering, audio ("A Game That Listens") and animation, not on layout.
- **Little Nightmares (Tarsier):**
  - The fixed, scrolling side camera gives a "doll's house" depth. Light is placed "based on what is important to see".
  - In LN2 the team "reworked the camera to offer more top views and in-depth character traversals".
  - The companion Six is not player-controlled ("players are never fully in charge of Six' destiny"), which allowed "longer puzzles that would rely on players ability to understand Six".
- **Ori (Moon Studios):** a layered painterly look with depth that stays "very readable" and serves gameplay, with foreground creatures passing along the lens. Rooms were blocked out first and painted afterwards.
- **Hollow Knight:**
  - GMTK Boss Keys: areas have distinct identities, and rooms tease the next zone with its materials (Greenpath leaves, Crystal Peak gems).
  - Each room is its own scene, entered through a brief fade.
- **Companions:**
  - **Elizabeth (Abercrombie, GDC 2014; GamesBeat):**
    - Like a soccer defender, she is kept on screen "between DeWitt and his destination", so the player notices what she does.
    - Theatre spotlighting for her cues.
    - She is quietly teleported to the player's side when left behind.
    - She is both companion and occasional leader. Abercrombie: "We're trying to create entertainment."
  - **Ellie (Dyckhoff, GDC 2014):** she must never break the bond ("you can never hate Ellie"): she is not noticed when running ahead and she is grabbed less often.
  - **Trico (genDESIGN):** his will is expressed through animation and staging rather than complex AI. Ueda: "we don't want our users to notice the intent of the designer."
- **General level design:**
  - Dan Taylor (GDC 2013): fun to navigate, leading with light and geometry, telling story without words.
  - The Level Design Book:
    - Landmarks must be functionally relevant.
    - Contrast creates importance ("a tall thing only seems special if surrounded by short things").
    - A vista plus a path makes an approach.
    - Teach, test, twist.
    - Traversal is a palate cleanser, not wasted time.
    - It also criticises leading lines as weak on their own, so use spatial organisation, light and landmarks rather than painted arrows.
  - Disney "weenie" (Scott Rogers): a visible goal that pulls you forward.
  - Totten: prospect and refuge, and narrow spaces alternating with open ones (compression and release).
  - GMTK, "Why Nathan Drake Doesn't Need a Compass": guide with light, colour, motion and geometry.

### 3. Room-width arithmetic at 190 px/s (estimated)
| Room width | Walkable span (x 40 to W−40) | One crossing | Visible views per room | Camera travel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 960 (today) | 880 px | 4.6 s | 1.35 | 249 px |
| 1440 (1.5 screens) | 1360 px | **7.2 s** | 2.0 | 729 px |
| 1680 | 1600 px | 8.4 s | 2.4 | 969 px |
| 1920 (2 screens) | 1840 px | **9.7 s** | 2.7 | 1209 px |

- One visible view (711 px) takes **3.7 s** to cross.
- Acceleration from the approved weight system will add roughly 0.1–0.2 s per start and stop.
- **Design limit:** at most ~4 s (~750 px, about one view) of walking without something new entering view, a state change or an interaction.
- At 1920 px, each crossing therefore needs 2–3 "something new" events.
- If the critical path crosses a room more than twice (as the corridor's breaker → relay → door does today), keep that room at ~1440. Use 1920 only for a room that is crossed once with a reveal in it.

### 4. Height arithmetic (estimated)
- **Without moving the camera:**
  - The engineer is ~70 world px tall on screen.
  - The head stays inside the HUD-clear band if the floor rise h ≤ ~150 px (440 − h − 70 ≥ 218).
  - A comfortable catwalk height is **96–120 px**. Anything higher needs vertical camera follow.
  - The touch camera y (`GAMEPLAY_CAMERA_Y_TOUCH`) must be rechecked.
- **Ramp lengths:**
  - A 96 px rise at 30° needs a ~166 px run (~0.9 s).
  - At ~1:3 (18°) it needs ~290 px (~1.5 s), the calmer choice.
  - Stay well below Godot's default `floor_max_angle` of 45°.
- **Godot setup (from the engine API, not tested here):**
  - Set `floor_constant_speed = true` so slopes do not change 190 px/s.
  - Raise `floor_snap_length` (about 8–16 px) so actors stay on the floor going down.
  - Draw stairs as stairs but give them ramp collision.
  - The x-only clamp in `m0_actor.gd` and the x-only WOLF targets must become per-room bounds.

### 5. Rules for WOLF//OVERRIDE (15)
1. **Width budget.**
   - Rooms are 1440–1920 world px, measured in walking seconds and not in pixels.
   - Never go more than ~4 s (one 711 px view) without a new sight, sound, state change or interaction.
   - The critical path crosses a room at most twice. Use 1920 only for single-crossing reveal rooms.
   - Measure the critical-path walking time in the blockout before any art, and add it to the scene test as a number.
2. **The landmark is the goal.**
   - Each room has one tall, distinct landmark (the exit door, shutter or blast door), and its silhouette is unique to the room.
   - It is visible from the entry or within the first ~1.5 s, through camera look-ahead.
   - Show the gate before you need to open it, with state lights on the gate itself (weenie, Taylor, LDB).
   - Tease the next room's material near the exit (Hollow Knight).
3. **Fill the walk with parallel action, not stations.**
   - Between beats, let the background move and react to state (Chahi): a fan, a leak, a lamp dying, light behind glass.
   - Stations sit off-centre at uneven spacing, not like cabinets in a row.
4. **Stage a reveal as occlude, approach, release.**
   - The thing to reveal starts hidden behind a wall edge, the foreground piece or darkness.
   - The approach narrows: low ceiling, tight framing.
   - Release on a cue region:
     - the camera eases toward the reveal with a cue-focus attractor;
     - an optional brief zoom-out from 1.35 to about 1.15–1.2 over ~0.5 s;
     - light or sound changes.
   - The player keeps control throughout, with no lock longer than ~1.5 s (Chahi's "brief" punctuation).
   - Put the reveal at about 55–70% of the room's width, so it pays off the walk and leaves room to act on it.
5. **Compression and release.**
   - Alternate a narrow, low space with a tall bay in each room (Totten).
   - The tall bay holds the reveal and the landmark.
   - The narrow passage holds the foreground piece and refuge spots, such as the junction alcove.
6. **Put the height change on the critical path, never as a fork.**
   - With only left and right input, the player cannot choose "up the stairs" at a junction. The ramp, stair or catwalk must be the path itself:
     - a rising floor; or
     - ramp up, catwalk, ramp down.
   - If a branch is ever needed, USE at the stair foot starts an auto-walk. That stays touch-friendly.
   - Every raised section must have a walkable way down, with no dead ends.
   - Never put a lethal hazard on a slope.
7. **Height is a vista.**
   - Use the catwalk as the approach view onto the room's reveal or hazard (prospect).
   - The floor below is the refuge or work level.
   - The rise should change what the player can see, not just the sprite's y.
8. **Camera.** Keep 1.35 as the base.
   - **Dual forward-focus look-ahead** of about 60–90 px in the walking direction, with a slow ~0.6 s switch so turning back does not whip the camera.
   - **Cue-focus attractors** on the next unfinished objective, the doorway and reveals, with overlapping rings for smooth handoffs.
   - **Vertical platform-snap:** re-target y only when the engineer has settled on a new floor height, with a dead zone of about 40 px, eased over about 0.5 s along ramps.
   - Always keep the walking floor line inside the HUD-clear band.
   - Shake stays on `offset`, as it is now.
9. **One foreground piece per room, placed between beats.**
   - Use a thin column, pipe, chains or a door frame, ≤ about 120 world px wide (≤ ~0.6 s behind it at walk speed).
   - Never place it within any station's interaction radius or at WOLF's stop points.
   - Fade it to about 35–50% alpha, or switch it to a silhouette, whenever it covers an actor.
   - Give it a job: it acts as the reveal shutter in rule 4, the compression in rule 5, or the doorway mask in rule 11.
   - Respect reduce-motion for its parallax.
10. **Readable depth.**
    - The gameplay plane has the highest contrast and the clearest silhouettes.
    - The background is darker and lower contrast and carries only parallel action.
    - Light the important things: light pools on objectives and dark gaps between them, which also fixes the audit's flat luma.
    - Never let the background compete with a hazard (Inside, Ori, Little Nightmares).
11. **Doorways are walk-through.**
    - Walking into the door trigger is enough. USE also works as a fallback.
    - The held direction carries through, including a touch hold.
    - Fade out about 0.2–0.25 s, hold black ≤ 0.15 s, fade in about 0.3 s, for ≤ ~0.7 s in total. Alternatively, the camera keeps panning at walk speed while the door-frame foreground masks the plate swap.
    - The engineer appears already walking 48–64 px inside the matching door on the opposite side (exit right, enter left).
    - Room tone crossfades through the transition so the world feels continuous (Inside).
    - Pause and Back work during it.
    - It never saves (Nathanial's decision).
    - The first view of the new room is safe: no lethal hazard within the first ~1 view (Oddworld's flip-screen lesson).
12. **WOLF's own lane.**
    - WOLF moves on authored routes: machine tops, pipes and the space under them.
    - Build these as Path2D or waypoint lanes he travels with authored hops and climbs, not physics jumps. He is not player-driven, so his animation carries his will (Trico).
    - Nothing on his lane is ever required. Anything he does up there has an engineer-side equivalent on the floor.
13. **WOLF stays visible, ahead and out of the way.**
    - When he leads, he stays on screen between the engineer and the goal (Elizabeth) and waits at the doorway he scouted, looking back.
    - When he follows, he never stands within a station's interaction radius and never covers the engineer. Add a test for this; the audit found seam x 418 against valve x 420, and mirror 520 against 520.
    - If he falls more than one view behind, he quietly catches up off screen.
    - He never causes a fail state (Ellie).
    - When he refuses, show it through staging (he stays on a machine top and turns away) while the engineer's route stays unchanged.
14. **Teach, test, twist, one idea per room.**
    - Each room introduces its core idea safely, tests it, then twists it once (LDB, Hayashida).
    - Corridor: routing power. Records: copying. Junction: pressure.
    - The Junction's twist already exists. The Corridor and Records each need one small twist through position or timing, not a new verb.
15. **Telegraph lethal space now that the engineer can die.**
    - A killing hazard is in view for at least ~1.5 s (~285 px of walking, look-ahead included) before it can reach the engineer.
    - Steam knockdowns warn by sound before they are seen.
    - Death teaches, as in Limbo, only with a nearby safe point (the safe-point model is being researched separately). Hide the threat's timing, never the way forward.

### 6. How the rules map onto the current beats (suggested, not prescriptive)
- **Corridor, about 1440:**
  - Entry and purge display.
  - Breaker at about 25%.
  - Relay at about 50%, under a pipe run that is WOLF's lane.
  - Then the narrow passage (foreground column) and a ramp up to a short catwalk that overlooks the sealed shutter. The shutter is the landmark and is visible from the start through look-ahead.
  - Safe point in the bay, separate from the exit doorway.
- **Records, about 1440–1680:**
  - Entry door, then the queue.
  - A dark aisle compression with a foreground stack end.
  - Reveal: the lit mirror bay plus a glass wall.
  - Mirror port with WOLF's spot 40–60 px off it, or on top of the stack.
  - A catwalk or stair down to the exit hatch with its own silhouette.
- **Junction, about 1920:**
  - The pressure line runs along the room as the leading feature.
  - Blast reveal at about 60%. The alcove is the refuge under a low ceiling. The sentry lane is on the floor, with a catwalk vantage over it before entry.
  - WOLF's seam position moves off the valve (about x 390 equivalent, or on the door side).
  - Bolt and hatch as the exit doorway.
- All beats and their saved state stay as they are; only positions and pacing change.

### 7. Evidence limits
- Several primary GDC talks are on the paywalled Vault (Dyckhoff, Abercrombie, Carlsen, Chahi, Taylor). Their points come from Game Developer, GamesBeat and Kill Screen coverage, not from the talks themselves.
- Taylor's full list of ten principles was not retrieved.
- The GMTK transcripts returned 403. The Hollow Knight and Nathan Drake points come from search summaries of those videos.
- The Inside points come from reviews and an analysis, not a Playdead layout talk; none was found.
- All timings and sizes in sections 3–5 are arithmetic or judgment, not measured play.

## Scope and evidence
- **What I read:** the full code in `wt-game/apps/game` (HEAD `1d60aa0`, clean worktree): `main.gd` (all 2,271 lines), `main.tscn` geometry, `m0_actor.gd`, `m0_state.gd`, `room_depth.gd`, `records_room.gd`, `junction_room.gd`, `sentry.gd`, `sentry_brain.gd`, `pressure_line.gd`, `drop_arm.gd`, `hazard.gd`, `floor_reflection.gd`, `hold_use.gd` and the positional parts of every test.
- **Also read:** `audit.json` (lv1, lv2, synth) and the judged part of `real-inventory-design.json`. I read the private context files but don't quote them; nothing in them conflicts with the decisions below.
- **Evidence level:** everything here comes from reading code. I ran nothing and played nothing, so none of it says anything about feel.
- **No edits.** I changed no files and made no commits.

## Headline: the cheapest safe model
Nathanial's rule, "one walkable height change per room", plus input that is left, right and USE only (no up), means **the floor should be a height field.** Each room's walkable floor is one polyline where y is a single value of x. Ramps, stairs and a catwalk you walk onto at one end and off at the other all fit this. A level the engineer can stand on with more floor underneath does not fit, because without an up input the player can't choose between the two. If a room really needs that, it should be a USE-triggered climb at a station.

What the height field keeps working:
- All of the pure logic (`SentryBrain`, `PressureLine`, `DropArm`, `HoldUse`) and every interaction-reach check stays x-based and correct.
- y is derived from `floor_y_at(x)`, so tests and saves can check it.
- Only WOLF leaves the height field, on authored routes (see section 5).

## 1. Every assumption of a 960 px room and a flat floor at y 440
**Physics and actors**
- **Floor body:** `main.tscn` lines 25–26 and 58–63. There is one shared `Floor` StaticBody2D, a 960×60 box at (480, 470), so its top is at y 440. Every room uses it: rooms are not separate spaces. All three sit at the same world origin and are only shown or hidden (`_sync_records_room` line 1892, `_sync_junction_room` line 1833).
- **Actor clamps:** `m0_actor.gd` clamps the follow target to x 40–920 (line 24) and clamps position to x 40–920 after `move_and_slide` (line 36).
  - Movement is x only, with a hand-rolled gravity (lines 31–34) and no floor-snap, max-slope or constant-speed settings.
  - The engineer's body is a 28×60 rectangle and WOLF's is 62×34 (`main.tscn` lines 31–35). A rectangle catches a corner on a ramp, and WOLF's long box will hover at one end.
- **Spawn heights:** the engineer spawns at y 410 and WOLF at y 423, both resting on 440 (`main.tscn` lines 89 and 113; `m0_state.gd` lines 24–25, 99–100, 131–132).
- **Corridor door:** a StaticBody2D in Main at (780, 374), 56×132 (`main.tscn` lines 65–70). It is not part of a room. All corridor stations, labels and status lights are also Main children with hard-coded y values (`main.tscn` lines 157–243). **The corridor is the only room without a room class.**
- **Sentry:** `sentry.gd` uses `FLOOR_Y = 440` (line 11) and pins `position.y = FLOOR_Y` every physics frame (lines 121, 128, 152). It moves on a flat rail.

**Interaction reach (all x-only, magic numbers in `main.gd`)**
- **Corridor:** purge display `x <= 230`; breaker `|x-350| <= 52`; relay `|x-605| <= 52`; safe point `|x-876| <= 52` (lines 1044–1053).
- **Records:** purge queue `|x-190| <= 58`; mirror port `|x-520| <= 58`; exit `|x-830| <= 58` (lines 1167–1209). WOLF at the mirror is `|x-520| <= 42` (line 1226).
- **Junction:** breaker, valve and door use `JunctionRoom.*_X ± 52/40`; the bolt uses `x >= BOLT_X-40`; the alcove uses `COVER_MIN/MAX_X` (lines 1291–1336). The valve hold uses the same check (line 1272).
- **Tutorial:** the same pattern repeats at lines 436–440.
- **Context hints and objectives:** they repeat every range again (lines 2078–2190), so each station's x lives in two or three places.

**WOLF targets**
- **All targets are single x values with -1 as "none":** `autonomous_target_x` (`m0_actor.gd` line 9) and `_wolf_target_x()` (lines 1934–1947).
- **Arrival is an exact ±4 px x check:** `RELAY_CONTACT_X` (lines 13, 434, 1093) and `WOLF_SEAM_X` (line 1444).
- **Fixed parking spots:** `WOLF_RUBBLE_X` and `WOLF_BAIT_X` (`junction_room.gd` lines 88–93).

**Hazards and the sentry lane**
- **Hurtboxes assume the floor at 440:**
  - `VentHazard` is `Rect2(264, 380, 72, 60)` (`junction_room.gd` line 311).
  - `CloudHazard` is `Rect2(MARK_X-52, 360, 104, 80)` (line 444).
- **Outcome tests are x ranges:** `PressureLine.is_in_blast` (360–540), `is_on_vent` (250–350), `DropArm.in_cloud`, `SentryBrain.is_exposed` and `touches`. They stay valid only while those spans are flat.
- **Lane constants:** `SentryBrain` has `RUBBLE_X` 540, `COVER` 556–584, patrol 624–840 and sight 180. `DropArm.MARK_X` is 700.
- **Placement helpers:** `JUNCTION_DOOR_LEFT_X` 452 (`m0_state.gd` line 16), `ENTRY/BREAKER/VENT/VALVE/DOOR/BOLT/HATCH_X`, `CHOICE_X`, `TANK_REST_Y` 340 and `GANTRY_Y` 120 (`junction_room.gd` lines 71–109).
- **Drawn geometry tied to 440:** the alcove spans y 318–440 (line 767), the doorway y 300–438 (line 774), the floor mark sits at `FLOOR_Y` (line 882), the rubble tick at y 439 (line 754), the hatch lift starts from `RoomDepth.FLOOR_Y` (line 696) and the landed tank uses `landed_tank_y` (line 563).
- **Records:** `EXIT_REST` (line 21), the light rects (lines 23–24) and the open-exit drawing at y 296–440 (lines 113–115). Main also draws the corridor's open-door line at y 434 (line 322).
- **Effects anchored to fixed points:** relay sparks (601, 390), door dust (780, 436), gate dust (115, 438) and exit sparks (830, 330) (lines 364–377). The intro uses fixed positions too (lines 480–496, 532, 541–548).

**Floor reflections and props**
- **Prop bases:** `RoomDepth.make_prop(..., base_y = FLOOR_Y)` (line 320).
- **Reflection mirror line:** `FloorReflection.floor_y` is fixed once at attach (line 38), and the mirror is a horizontal line through the feet (line 66). The reflection travels with an actor because it is a sibling inside the actor, but on a ramp it cuts into the slope, and on a grated catwalk it shouldn't exist at all.
- **Labels:** station labels sit at fixed y 276, 309 or 313.

**`room_depth.gd` (plates, parallax and near strips)**
- **Constants:** `ROOM_WIDTH = 960` and `FLOOR_Y = 440` (lines 15–16).
- **Plate scale:** plates are always drawn exactly room-wide, using `ROOM_WIDTH / texture width` (lines 246–248). The plates are 1920×1080, drawn at 0.5. Stretching them to a wider room also scales them up vertically against the actors, so **wider rooms need new wider plates; the current plates can't be reused stretched.**
- **Bleeds and near strips:**
  - The right bleed is anchored at `ROOM_WIDTH` (line 212).
  - The near layer holds only two edge strips: the left strip, and the same strip mirrored at `ROOM_WIDTH + overhang` (lines 172–175, 217–223). There is **no mid-room foreground piece**.
- **Everything else is sized to 960:** the base fill is 960+120 by 680 (line 234), the dust emitter sits at (480, 300) with extents 500×150 (lines 281–283), and haze and lamps are fractions of the far plate.
- **Parallax:** the far plate has x scroll 0.9 and y scroll 1.0, so there is no vertical parallax. Its width only covers the 249 px of camera travel; a 1440 px room moves the far plate by about 0.1 × the extra travel, so the far plate needs overhang.

rooms.concept:
"Up and out of containment." The room is 1680 world px (1.75 screens) with walkable x 40-1640. It is crossed once, left to right. The engineer starts on the low deck of WOLF's containment bay, where the story begins behind a slammed lockdown shutter. One landmark rises through the ceiling and can be seen from the handover: the COOLANT RELAY TOWER, which is also the relay the choice is about.

The first half teaches the verbs on one flat floor:
- walk
- tap USE (purge display)
- hold USE (optional log screen)
- the two choice buttons (WOLF's relay question at the breaker)

Cause and effect stay on one screen. Arming the breaker turns the tower's crown blue in the same frame, and the sealed door stands beside the tower.

Once the seal rises:
1. The engineer climbs one gentle stair (96 px up at 18 degrees) and passes behind a dark foreground bulkhead rib (compression).
2. They come out onto a grated catwalk where a long observation window reveals the archive stack below. Its rack lights are going dark in a slow sweep: the purge, physically happening (release).
3. WOLF took his own pipe route and is already at the window looking.
4. A warm SAFE POINT alcove follows (refuge), then a real walk-through doorway into Records Access.

Every current beat and its state is kept:
- purge display
- breaker with the relay_disagreement choice and arming
- relay (WOLF cooperate or engineer fallback, relay_refused)
- seal (door_open)
- safe point (checkpoint_reached)
- enter_records

What changes:
- The second USE at the safe point becomes walking through the exit door.
- Stations are re-spaced so no stretch of walking runs longer than about 1.6 s without something new.

Tone: strange and procedural. Machines report, lights follow state, nothing in the room can hurt you yet.

Evidence labels: everything here was designed from reading code and the review files. Nothing was built, rendered or played, so every number is a blockout starting point that has to be played by hand (AGENT.md).

rooms.concept: "Down into the stacks." The engineer comes in high, on a grated service gallery. The purge queue is right by the door, so the first job happens at once. From the doorway you can already see the landmark, the mirror core: a floor-to-ceiling column of cold blue light at the right edge of the first view. One steel stair leads down to the vault floor. The mirror port sits at the core's foot, and the existing WOLF-readout or manual-port choice happens there. Past the core, the engineer slips behind a near stack end and finds the reveal: the purged aisle. It is a long run of rack bays with empty cartridge slots and dark LEDs, and the only working lamp hangs over the archive lift hatch that leads to the Junction. WOLF takes his own high road the whole way: first the back rack tops, then the drive housing, then an overhead cable bridge. He gets there first and waits by the hatch. The engineer's floor never needs any of it. The tone is the quiet valley: gallery compression, release down the stair into the tall vault, then compression again in the dark aisle before the Junction peak. There are no hazards and no new story text. The beats and their state are unchanged (enter_records, preserve_purge_trace, preserve_mirror_trace(wolf|manual), complete_chapter, enter_junction); only positions and pacing change. Width is 1440 (1.5 screens, two plate segments). The room is crossed once, but 1920 would add about 2.5 s of walking with nothing new to fill it. Estimated critical path is about 6.9 s plus acceleration, against about 3.7 s today, and no stretch goes longer than about 1.1 s without a new sight, sound, state or interaction. rooms.hazards_and_death:

- The gallery lip has a kick plate, the stair has a handrail, and the bridge and rack tops are WOLF-only.

- a cartridge eject clack in the aisle

rooms.concept:
A 1440 px (1.5-screen) two-chamber room you cross once, going down and then right.

- **West chamber (pressure works):** the engineer comes out of the Records connector onto a raised grated landing (y 344) that overlooks it. A 1:3 stair takes them down to the wet deck (y 440).
- **Pressure beat:** the breaker, relief vent, valve and sealed blast door keep today's spacing exactly. The whole block is moved +480 px, so the tuned 6 s build, the 3 turns and the 1 s fuse need no retuning.
- **East chamber (sentry lane):** it sits behind a full-height bulkhead and stays dark and framed out until the door blows. The blast is the reveal: dust clears, the lane lamps come on left to right, and the hanging tank under the gantry swings into view while the sentry's eye wakes.
- **After the blast:** the lane block (rubble line, ARM PANEL alcove, mark, patrol, exit bolt, hatch) also keeps today's relative geometry, moved +480.
- **WOLF:** he goes his own high way. He runs a pipe bridge at landing height while the engineer takes the stair, reads the seam from the valve housing top, takes cover behind the foreground coolant main during the fuse, perches on the rubble, then leads to the hatch.
- **Tempo:** prospect (landing), compression (stair foot under the coolant main), peak 1 (blast), reveal and valley (lane wakes), peak 2 (tank drop), relax (bolt and hatch).
- **Height rule:** the floor is one height field, y = floor_y_at(x). Every hazard, choice and station sits on the flat y-440 span, so all x-only logic (PressureLine, SentryBrain, DropArm, HoldUse) stays valid with a constant offset.

Critical-path walk is about 8.5 s, against about 6 s today. No stretch is longer than about 3.2 s without a new sight, sound or state change.

All of these routes are WOLF's own choice and authored as route nodes, not single x targets. The engineer's path never waits on any of them.

- **W1, entry scout (high route):**

  5. He stays perched above the engineer while they crank.
- **W2, fuse cover:** on SEAL CHARGED he jumps down and runs to the stair foot behind the coolant main (about x 585). The occluder fades and he peeks out after the blast.
- **W3, rubble perch:** after the blast he climbs onto the rubble heap top (x 925-950, about y 405), WOLF_RUBBLE_X moved and raised. He refuses to cross the rubble and looks toward the lane, and he is never in the engineer's CHOICE_X footprint.

plan.summary_plain:
This is a plan for the three wider rooms and for the new title and hero art you asked for. Nothing has been built, rendered or played, so every number is a starting point.

1. The title comes first. Codex paints one new key art of the first room (the containment bay and the relay tower). It replaces the game's title screen, the website hero, the share card and the README image in one pass.
2. Next we build the shared room system, with no visible change in the game.
3. Then the corridor becomes a plain grey version you can play, and after that it gets painted. Records and the Junction follow the same steps.

I fixed where the three room drafts disagreed: there is now one stair size, one catwalk height, one door kit and fade, one camera rule, one set of WOLF route names, and no saving at doors. The Records exit becomes a lift, because the Junction starts higher. Total effort is about 31 working days.
shared_tech: 1. RoomProfile data, one resource per room and the single source of truth: width; floor polyline giving floor_y_at(x); a surface map (plate, wet plate, tread, grating, damp tile); stations with reach; pickups; doors; safe points; occluder rects; camera attractors; state limits; WOLF route graph. Station x values for interaction, tutorial, hints and objectives all read from it. Today each lives in 2-3 places in main.gd (lines 436-440, 1044-1053, 1167-1209, 2078-2190).

2. CorridorRoom class, extracted from main.gd and main.tscn (door at 780,374, stations, labels and lights are Main children today), so all three rooms are room classes. JunctionRoom gets a logic origin of 480, so PressureLine, SentryBrain, DropArm and their tests keep their current numbers.
3. Per-room floor collision built from the polyline: a StaticBody2D or CollisionPolygon2D per room replaces the shared 960x60 Floor in main.tscn. Stairs are drawn as treads but collide as one ramp.

4. Actor movement: capsule shapes for the engineer (replacing 28x60) and WOLF (replacing 62x34, or a two-ray foot probe); floor_constant_speed = true; floor_snap_length 12; engine is_on_floor in place of the hand-rolled gravity; per-room bounds [40, W-40] in place of 40-920. The approved weight/acceleration lands here. Sentry FLOOR_Y pinning becomes floor_y_at.

5. Camera rig: Camera2D limits [355.6, W-355.6] in place of the 960 clamp; 80 px look-ahead; one attractor system (cap 120 px, never moves the engineer); vertical follow at 50% of floor height; per-state limit override (Junction pre-blast); Reduced Motion halving; CHAPTER_CLOSE_CAMERA computed per room as (W - 480/1.55, 352). Impact shake keeps Camera2D.offset.

6. RoomDepth v2: room width from the profile in place of ROOM_WIDTH 960; plate scale fixed at 0.5 (2 src px per room px); shared walkway row 776 for every new plate (mid_top 52); far Parallax2D scroll_offset centred on the room; a list of near pieces (texture region plus world x); edge strips narrowed to 24 px or removed wherever a doorway sits. FloorReflection switches by surface, with its mirror line taken from floor_y_at.

7. Doorway kit and carry-through: frame, leaf sprite, lamp and trigger; 0.2 s walk-in, 0.3 s fade, room switch and camera cut while black, 0.3 s fade-in with auto-walk, room-tone crossfade as the sound bridge; the tween pauses with the tree. Each room entry sets an in-memory restore point, never a disk save. The lift variant adds a 96 px rise thunk during the black.

8. WOLF route graph. Node kinds: FLOOR, PERCH, RUN, HOP, CLIMB, COVER, DOOR_WAIT, LEAD. He moves at 220 px/s. Arrival is node index reached (6 px, 1.5 s timeout), replacing the ±4 px checks (RELAY_CONTACT_X, WOLF_SEAM_X). Catch-up warp happens only when both his position and his target are off-screen. The pose layer covers hops and lands, with crouch and squash on landing.

9. Save v5, shared with the evidence case: room_id plus x validated against the profile bounds, y derived from floor_y_at (or a WOLF node id while he is on a ledge); legacy corridor positions (x 824-920) migrate to the new safe point; spawn coordinates move out of M0State into the room data; door saves removed (main.gd:1149 on Records entry and :1288 Junction autosave A).
10. Audio hooks: profile surfaces drive the approved per-surface footsteps; per-room room tone loops; the carry-through crossfades them.

11. Headless profile lint and estimator tests: no reach overlaps; no station or pickup on a slope; the occluder never covers a reach, hazard, choice point or door at sampled camera x (touch and desktop y); no WOLF floor stand node inside an active reach; door sills match across each join unless the door is a lift; spawn outside every reach; critical-path walking time per room and longest gap without an event.
